content:
A Laredo man will spend the next 21 years in federal prison for a fentanyl deal that ended with a man's death in a Laredo hotel room, according to the Laredo Morning Times' reporting on the sentencing.

Rene Antonio Melendez, 34, pleaded guilty on June 29 to conspiracy to distribute fentanyl resulting in death. U.S. District Judge Diana Saldana sentenced him to 252 months — 21 years — in federal prison, to be followed by three years of supervised release.

The case traces back to March 11, 2023, when law enforcement responded to a Laredo hotel after a report of an unresponsive man. The victim's friend told authorities the man had consumed a substance known as "White China" and stopped breathing. Investigators recovered a baggie containing fentanyl from the hotel room, and the medical examiner later determined the victim died of acute fentanyl toxicity.

According to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas, text messages showed the victim had arranged to buy $80 worth of drugs through Melendez and was directed to a meeting spot off San Bernardo Avenue. Cellphone records, witness interviews, and historical cell-site data established that Melendez was the one who supplied the fentanyl. Later that day, Melendez sent the victim a text message asking about the drugs; shortly afterward, the victim's friend called 911 to report he was not breathing.

The case was investigated as part of a Homeland Security Task Force investigation and prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Leslie Ann Cortez. Melendez remains in custody pending transfer to a federal Bureau of Prisons facility.

Fentanyl — a synthetic opioid far more potent than heroin — has driven a wave of overdose deaths across South Texas in recent years, and federal prosecutors in the Southern District of Texas have made overdose-death cases a priority.

Sources: Laredo Morning Times (Oct. 20, 2026); U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas press release (Oct. 20, 2026).

title: Laredo man sentenced to 21 years in federal prison for fentanyl deal that led to overdose death
